title: Patchwork Isles
tagline: Paint a scrap of fabric, sew it into a sea chart, then sail a cloth boat round it
summary: WaveFunctionCollapse's OverlappingModel learns every 3×3 piece of a twelve-square scrap you paint and sews a 72×48 sea chart from it, stitch by stitch, knotting and unpicking when it contradicts itself; a second Admiralty mode builds charts from eleven coastline tiles with the SimpleTiledModel. The finished chart is checked for reachable harbours and becomes the map of a short sailing game with wind, fog, shoals and a season to beat.

controls.keys: click and drag, or arrow keys + Space

features: OverlappingModel learns the 2×2 or 3×3 pieces of a painted 12×12 scrap (1, 2, 4 or 8 turns and mirrors) and sews a 72×48 chart
The collapse is shown live: iterate() runs in small batches each tick, settled cells pop in as fabric squares and pencil shading shows how constrained the rest still are
Contradictions appear as knots; retries run at speed with generate() and the first clean seed is replayed with iterate(), so you still watch it being sewn
Each finished chart is judged: harbours must sit on the open sea and be spread out, otherwise the loom retries (up to 14 tries) and says why
SimpleTiledModel sews an Admiralty chart from 11 coastline pieces whose 2×2 bitmaps are the chart cells, with neighbour rules generated by matching corners
Wrap edges (periodic output), piece size and symmetry are live options; sample, sewing and voyage seeds are shareable in the URL and charts export as PNG
The sewn terrain is the game map: shallows slow you, shoals by rocks ground a boat under full sail, harbours restock you and reveal more ports
lessons: esm.sh turns the CommonJS package into named exports (OverlappingModel, SimpleTiledModel). Load it through an import map at the exact version.

The constructor is cheap but the first iterate()/generate() allocates the wave, at about 0.36 MB per pattern for a 72×48 chart (arrays of arrays). Read model.T after constructing and refuse samples that make too many patterns. Also, clear() throws on a model that has never iterated.

Don't call graphics() every frame on an unfinished OverlappingModel: it loops cells × N² × patterns. To animate, read model.sumsOfOnes and model.wave to find cells that have settled, and call graphics() once at the end.
With N=3 on a 12×12 sample, non-periodic input contradicts almost every time. Design samples that tile, and keep periodicInput on.

iterate(n, rng) gives the same result however you split n, as long as the seeded rng is the same. So you can search seeds quickly with generate() and replay the winning one with iterate() for the animation. In SimpleTiledModel, generate neighbour pairs from the library's own rotated tile bitmaps, because a wrong symmetry letter silently gives wrong rules.
deviations: The 'periodic edges' option controls periodic output (the chart wraps east–west and north–south); periodic input is always on, because in testing non-periodic input with 3×3 pieces on a 12×12 scrap contradicted on nearly every try. To keep a round at 2–5 minutes, at most 7 harbours stay as ports of call, spread across the chart; the other harbour clusters are turned into beach, and the workroom says how many. To protect memory, the loom refuses scraps that cut into more than 360 patterns (350 on devices reporting 2 GB or less) and explains how to simplify them. The Admiralty mode is tuned with three coast presets (tile weights) instead of a painted scrap.
browser_support: any modern browser (ES modules, Canvas 2D, WebAudio); the library loads from esm.sh, so it needs a connection
checked: Played with scripts/inspect.mjs at 1440×900 and 390×844 using real input: mouse clicks and drags on desktop (Play, ready scrap, painting on the frame, number keys for fabrics, Sew, Skip ahead, Set sail, arrow keys to steer and trim, clicking the sea to set a course, C for the chart view, Esc to pause and resume), and taps, touch drags and held touch buttons on the phone (painting, recovering from a scrap that knotted 13 times in 14 tries, steering with the thumb pads, sail buttons, tapping a course, chart and pause buttons). Each round then ran to the end screen with a small autopilot driven through window.__game.input(), and probes confirmed every state change (title, sewing, workroom, playing, chart, paused, over). An 11-chart autopilot batch (8 patchwork charts and 3 Admiralty charts) won every voyage, in 67 to 170 seconds of sim time with 2 to 7 days to spare. Same seed and same inputs give an identical snapshot. Also checked: keyboard-only menus (Tab, Enter, Escape returning focus, arrow keys and Space painting the scrap), reduced motion, the muted attract mode inside an iframe, 2560×1440, zero console errors and failed requests, and no sideways overflow at any size. Sample scraps were tuned in Node against the library source for pattern counts, contradiction rates, harbour reachability and island-shape variety. Every screenshot was reviewed.
